items.subject: california
items.title: We live in California
items.summary: California is a state in the United States. It sits on the West Coast, next to the Pacific Ocean.

items.subject: california
items.title: Golden poppy, our state flower
items.summary: The golden poppy is California's state flower. It is bright orange-yellow and grows wild in fields and on hills.

items.subject: california
items.title: California quail, our state bird
items.summary: The California quail is our state bird. It has a little curved feather on its head that bobs when it walks.

items.subject: california
items.title: Redwoods, our state tree
items.summary: Redwoods are California's state tree. Some are taller than a skyscraper, and they can live for hundreds of years.

items.subject: california
items.title: The grizzly bear on our flag
items.summary: The California grizzly bear is our state animal. It is on our flag, even though grizzlies no longer live wild in California.

items.subject: california
items.title: Our California flag
items.summary: The state flag has a big brown bear, a red star, and a red stripe on white. It says California Republic.

items.subject: california
items.title: Ocean and beaches
items.summary: California has a long coast on the Pacific Ocean. Beaches have sand, waves, tide pools, and sea animals.

items.subject: california
items.title: Mountains, forests, and deserts
items.summary: California has tall mountains with snow, big forests, and hot dry deserts. Many different places are all in one state.

items.subject: california
items.title: Weather where we live
items.summary: Much of California has warm, dry summers and cooler, rainy winters. Mountains can get lots of snow.

items.subject: california
items.title: Community helpers
items.summary: Firefighters, police officers, teachers, and doctors help keep our neighborhoods safe and healthy.

items.subject: california
items.title: Earthquake: drop, cover, hold on
items.summary: If the ground shakes, drop to the floor, get under a sturdy table, and hold on until the shaking stops.

items.subject: california
items.title: California words
items.summary: Words about our state that are fun to say and know.

items.subject: california
items.title: Our state song
items.summary: The state song is I Love You, California. It was made the official state song in 1989.

items.subject: california
items.title: Our motto: Eureka
items.summary: Eureka is California's state motto. It is a Greek word that means I have found it, and it reminds us of the Gold Rush.

items.subject: california
items.title: Whales, turtles, and garibaldi
items.summary: California picks symbols from the sea too. The gray whale is the state marine mammal, and the bright orange garibaldi is the state marine fish.

items.subject: california
items.title: Golden trout and desert tortoise
items.summary: The golden trout is the state freshwater fish and the desert tortoise is the state reptile. Both live in very different places.

items.subject: california
items.title: Saber-toothed cat fossil
items.summary: The saber-toothed cat, Smilodon, is California's state fossil. Many of its bones were found in the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.

items.subject: california
items.title: State rock and state mineral
items.summary: Serpentine is California's state rock, and gold is the state mineral. Gold is why California is called the Golden State.

items.subject: california
items.title: The Pacific coast
items.summary: California's western edge touches the Pacific Ocean. Cities like San Diego, Los Angeles, and San Francisco are on the coast.

items.subject: california
items.title: Finding California on a map
items.summary: California is on the west side of the United States. Oregon is north, Nevada and Arizona are east, and Mexico is south.

items.subject: california
items.title: Rules and laws
items.summary: Rules keep people safe and fair. Laws are rules for a whole city or state, and leaders help make them.

items.subject: california
items.title: Sacramento is our capital
items.summary: Sacramento is the capital of California. The governor works there, and the state Capitol building is where lawmakers meet.

items.subject: california
items.title: Redwoods and giant sequoias
items.summary: The state tree includes two kinds. Coast redwoods grow in foggy forests near the coast, and giant sequoias grow on Sierra Nevada mountainsides.

items.subject: california
items.title: Fire safety at home
items.summary: Practice a family plan: know two ways out, pick a meeting spot, and never play with matches. If you smell smoke, tell a grown-up and go outside.

items.subject: california
items.title: California symbol words
items.summary: Words for talking about our state symbols.

items.subject: california
items.title: Cities, towns, and neighborhoods
items.summary: California has big cities, small towns, and farms. A community is the people and places close to where you live.

items.subject: california
items.title: Regions of California
items.summary: California has a coast, a long flat Central Valley, the Sierra Nevada mountains, and deserts in the south and east.

items.subject: california
items.title: Highest mountain: Mount Whitney
items.summary: Mount Whitney in the Sierra Nevada is the tallest mountain in the lower 48 states, about 14,500 feet high.

items.subject: california
items.title: Death Valley
items.summary: Death Valley is a hot, dry desert in eastern California. It has the lowest spot in North America, at Badwater Basin.

items.subject: california
items.title: Lake Tahoe
items.summary: Lake Tahoe is a huge, clear, deep mountain lake on the California and Nevada border. People swim, boat, and ski nearby.

items.subject: california
items.title: Big rivers
items.summary: The Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers flow through the Central Valley. They bring water to farms and cities.

items.subject: california
items.title: Farms and food
items.summary: Many fruits, vegetables, and nuts you eat grow on California farms, especially in the Central Valley. Almonds, grapes, and strawberries are examples.

items.subject: california
items.title: California Native peoples
items.summary: Many different Native peoples have lived in California for thousands of years, and they still live here today. Each has its own language and traditions.

items.subject: california
items.title: Chumash and the tomol
items.summary: The Chumash live along the Santa Barbara coast. They traditionally built tomols, plank boats, and Chumash people still build and paddle them today.

items.subject: california
items.title: Earthquake preparedness
items.summary: Families can keep water, flashlights, and snacks in a kit. Practice drop, cover, and hold on, and know a safe spot in each room.

items.subject: california
items.title: What does a governor do?
items.summary: The governor is the leader of the state. The governor signs or vetoes new laws and helps run state agencies.

items.subject: california
items.title: California place words
items.summary: Words about California's land and water.

items.subject: california
items.title: Many nations, many cultures
items.summary: California had more than 100 Native languages, and many peoples such as Yurok, Pomo, Miwok, Chumash, and Tongva. They are not all alike.

items.subject: california
items.title: Yurok, river, and redwoods
items.summary: The Yurok live along the Klamath River in northern California. Salmon, redwood canoes, and ceremonies are important to Yurok life.

items.subject: california
items.title: Pomo baskets
items.summary: Pomo weavers are famous for beautiful, tightly woven baskets, some decorated with feathers and beads. Pomo artists keep the craft alive today.

items.subject: california
items.title: Acorns as food
items.summary: Many California Native peoples gathered acorns, ground them into flour, and rinsed out bitter parts to make soups and breads.

items.subject: california
items.title: Tongva of the Los Angeles area
items.summary: The Tongva have lived in the Los Angeles Basin and nearby islands for thousands of years. Tongva people keep their culture and language alive today.

items.subject: california
items.title: Native peoples today
items.summary: California Native communities are modern and living. Many tribes have governments, schools, and cultural programs, and share their own stories.

items.subject: california
items.title: California's big regions
items.summary: The coast, Central Valley, Sierra Nevada, and deserts each have different land, weather, and plants.

items.subject: california
items.title: Climate in California
items.summary: Much of California has a Mediterranean climate: dry summers and wet winters. Mountains are colder and deserts are hotter and drier.

items.subject: california
items.title: California landmarks
items.summary: The Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937. Yosemite, Mount Whitney, and the Pacific Coast are other famous places.

items.subject: california
items.title: Local government
items.summary: Cities have a mayor and city council. Counties have a board of supervisors. They run parks, libraries, fire stations, and more.

items.subject: california
items.title: Three parts of state government
items.summary: Like our country, California has three branches: lawmakers make laws, the governor carries them out, and judges explain them.

items.subject: california
items.title: Wildfire safety
items.summary: Wildfires can spread fast in dry weather. Families should have a go-bag, a plan, and listen to leaders if told to evacuate.

items.subject: california
items.title: Redwood forests
items.summary: Coast redwoods grow in cool, foggy places in northern California. Parks help protect them and the animals that live there.

items.subject: california
items.title: California history starter words
items.summary: Words you will meet when learning about California's story.

items.subject: california
items.title: A changing state
items.summary: Fourth graders study how California changed over time, from Native peoples, to Spanish and Mexican rule, to the Gold Rush and today.

items.subject: california
items.title: Land shaped Native ways of life
items.summary: Native peoples used what was near them. Coastal, forest, valley, mountain, and desert communities differed in food, homes, and tools.

items.subject: california
items.title: Many peoples, not one story
items.summary: Chumash, Miwok, Yurok, Pomo, Tongva, Kumeyaay, and many others each have their own history, so one name does not fit all.

items.subject: california
items.title: Spanish explorers reach California
items.summary: In 1542 Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo sailed along the California coast for Spain. Later Spain sent soldiers and priests to settle it.

items.subject: california
items.title: The California missions
items.summary: Between 1769 and 1823 the Spanish built 21 missions from San Diego to Sonoma, linked by a road called El Camino Real.

items.subject: california
items.title: Missions and Native peoples
items.summary: Missions changed Native lives. Many people were made to live and work there, and disease and loss of land harmed Native families.

items.subject: california
items.title: Mexico and the ranchos
items.summary: Mexico became independent from Spain in 1821. Missions ended and the government gave large ranchos for cattle to settlers.

items.subject: california
items.title: The Bear Flag Revolt
items.summary: In 1846 American settlers in Sonoma raised a flag with a bear and declared a California Republic. Soon the Mexican-American War reached California.

items.subject: california
items.title: Gold at Sutter's Mill
items.summary: In January 1848, James Marshall found gold in the American River at Coloma, setting off the Gold Rush.

items.subject: california
items.title: The forty-niners
items.summary: In 1849 tens of thousands of people came for gold from many places. Most miners did not get rich, but many stayed.

items.subject: california
items.title: Gold Rush effects on Native peoples
items.summary: The Gold Rush brought violence, disease, and loss of homelands for many Native Californians, causing huge population loss.

items.subject: california
items.title: Becoming a state
items.summary: California became the 31st state on September 9, 1850. Sacramento became the permanent capital in 1854.

items.subject: california
items.title: The transcontinental railroad
items.summary: Sacramento was the start of the Central Pacific Railroad. In 1869 it met the Union Pacific in Utah, linking California to the East.

items.subject: california
items.title: Chinese workers and railroads
items.summary: Thousands of Chinese immigrants built the railroad through the Sierra Nevada. They faced danger and unfair treatment.

items.subject: california
items.title: How a bill becomes a law
items.summary: A lawmaker suggests a bill. Committees and both houses vote, then the governor signs it to become law, or vetoes it.

items.subject: california
items.title: California history words
items.summary: Key words for fourth grade California history.

items.subject: california
items.title: State and national constitutions
items.summary: California has its own constitution, and the United States has one too. Both set up governments and protect rights.

items.subject: california
items.title: The California Legislature
items.summary: The Legislature has a Senate with 40 members and an Assembly with 80. They meet in the Capitol in Sacramento.

items.subject: california
items.title: Ballot propositions
items.summary: Voters can decide some laws directly by voting on propositions. Citizens can collect signatures to put an idea on the ballot.

items.subject: california
items.title: 58 counties
items.summary: California is divided into 58 counties, and each has cities and towns. Counties help with roads, health, and elections.

items.subject: california
items.title: Why California grew
items.summary: People came for gold, land, farms, jobs, and weather. California is the most populous state.

items.subject: california
items.title: Central Valley farming
items.summary: The Central Valley grows lots of America's fruit, nuts, and vegetables. Farmworkers help harvest the food we eat.

items.subject: california
items.title: Moving water
items.summary: Most rain and snow falls in the north, but many people live in the south. Aqueducts and dams move water to farms and cities.

items.subject: california
items.title: Angel Island
items.summary: From 1910 to 1940, Angel Island in San Francisco Bay was an immigration station where many Asian immigrants were held and questioned.

items.subject: california
items.title: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta
items.summary: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta helped found a union for farmworkers and worked peacefully for fair pay and better conditions.

items.subject: california
items.title: John Muir
items.summary: John Muir came to California from Scotland and explored the Sierra Nevada. He helped protect Yosemite and founded the Sierra Club.

items.subject: california
items.title: Sally Ride
items.summary: Sally Ride, a Californian physicist, became the first American woman in space in 1983.

items.subject: california
items.title: Jackie Robinson
items.summary: Jackie Robinson grew up in Pasadena, California. He broke Major League Baseball's color barrier in 1947.

items.subject: california
items.title: Why earthquakes happen
items.summary: Earth's plates slowly slide, and the San Andreas Fault runs through California. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake caused a big fire.

items.subject: california
items.title: California government words
items.summary: Words about how California governs itself.

items.subject: california
items.title: Native California and early peoples
items.summary: Native peoples have lived in California for thousands of years, building complex societies with trade networks and careful care of the land.

items.subject: california
items.title: California and the world
items.summary: People from around the world, including China, Mexico, and Europe, have shaped California's cities and culture.

items.subject: california
items.title: Pacific trade
items.summary: California's ports connect to Asia and beyond. Trade across the Pacific shapes jobs and communities.

items.subject: california
items.title: World connections vocabulary
items.summary: Words that link California to the wider world.

items.subject: california
items.title: Caring for land and water
items.summary: Cultural burning, fishing, and gathering practices of Native peoples show long-term care of the land.

items.subject: california
items.title: Spanish empire in California
items.summary: The mission system was part of Spain's empire, which tried to claim lands and convert Native peoples.

items.subject: california
items.title: Trade and the Pacific
items.summary: Ships carried hides, tallow, and later gold. California trade tied into world markets.

items.subject: california
items.title: Chinese labor in California
items.summary: Chinese workers built railroads and farms, then faced laws like the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act.

items.subject: california
items.title: Port cities
items.summary: San Francisco and Los Angeles grew as ports. Immigrants arrived there from across the Pacific.

items.subject: california
items.title: Migration vocabulary
items.summary: Words for how people move and trade.

items.subject: california
items.title: Native trade networks
items.summary: Native peoples traded shells, obsidian, and baskets across long distances.

items.subject: california
items.title: California and Mexico
items.summary: Mexican California connected to Mexico City, ranchos, and Pacific trade.

items.subject: california
items.title: California in the Mexican-American War
items.summary: From 1846 to 1848 the U.S. and Mexico fought. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave California to the United States.

items.subject: california
items.title: 1849 Constitution and statehood
items.summary: Delegates met in Monterey in 1849 and wrote a constitution. California became a state in 1850 as a free state.

items.subject: california
items.title: Native peoples and U.S. rule
items.summary: After 1848 many Native Californians lost land and lives. In 2019 the governor formally apologized for the state's role.

items.subject: california
items.title: Dust Bowl migration
items.summary: In the 1930s many families from the Plains moved to California for farm work, often facing hardship.

items.subject: california
items.title: World War II in California
items.summary: California factories and shipyards grew in WWII. Japanese Americans were unfairly incarcerated.

items.subject: california
items.title: Braceros and farm labor
items.summary: From 1942 to 1964 the bracero program brought Mexican workers to U.S. farms. Later farmworker organizing improved conditions.

items.subject: california
items.title: Initiative, referendum, recall
items.summary: In 1911 California voters gained the initiative, referendum, and recall, giving citizens more direct power.

items.subject: california
items.title: Statehood and civics words
items.summary: Words about California's path to statehood and government.
